problemText: A sequence of rock layers has not been disturbed by folding, tilting, or faulting. According to the law of superposition, which layer must be the oldest?
choices: The layer at the top of the stack
The layer in the middle of the stack
The layer at the bottom of the stack
The layer with the hardest rock type
hints: The law of superposition applies specifically to undisturbed layers.
Each layer was laid down on top of what was already there.

problemText: A cliff shows four flat, undisturbed rock layers. From bottom to top, they are basalt, granite, marble, and slate. What is the correct order from oldest to youngest?
choices: Marble, slate, basalt, granite
Slate, marble, granite, basalt
Granite, basalt, slate, marble
Basalt, granite, marble, slate
hints: The layers are flat and undisturbed, so superposition applies without exception.
The bottom layer was laid down first, and each layer above it is younger.

problemText: A road cut displays three flat layers of sandstone, shale, and limestone stacked one on top of another. A narrow crack filled with igneous rock cuts through the sandstone and shale but does not reach the limestone above. The limestone lies flat and unbroken across the top of the crack. What does this tell you about when the igneous rock formed?
choices: It is younger than the sandstone and shale but older than the limestone
It is younger than all three layers because it cuts through two of them
It is older than all three layers because it filled a crack that existed first
It is the same age as the sandstone because it cuts through it
hints: A cutting feature is younger than what it cuts and older than what lies unbroken over it.
The key detail is that the limestone sits unbroken across the top of the crack.

problemText: A hillside shows four rock layers tilted at a steep angle, all sloping the same direction. From the lowest position on the hillside to the highest, the rocks are mudstone, then sandstone, then shale, then limestone. A student says the mudstone must be the oldest because it is lowest on the hillside. Explain why this reasoning is incomplete and put the layers in correct order from oldest to youngest.
choices: The student is correct; the mudstone is oldest because it is lowest, even though the layers are tilted at a steep angle
The layers were deposited flat and tilted later; the order from oldest to youngest is mudstone, sandstone, shale, limestone
The principle of original horizontality does not apply to tilted layers, so their ages cannot be determined without radiometric dating methods
The tilting means the highest layer on the hillside must be the oldest because layers tilt in the direction of uplift
hints: Remember that original horizontality tells you the layers started flat before anything moved them.
Tilted layers can still be ordered by superposition, but you cannot assume lowest position means oldest.

problemText: A cliff section contains five features: a layer of sandstone, a layer of shale above it, a layer of limestone above that, a fault cutting diagonally through all three layers, and a layer of coal sitting flat and unbroken on top of the fault. Put these five features in order from oldest to youngest.
choices: Sandstone, shale, limestone, coal, fault
Fault, sandstone, shale, limestone, coal
Sandstone, shale, limestone, fault, coal
Coal, fault, limestone, shale, sandstone
hints: Start by ordering the three layers that are undisturbed; then use Rule 3 to place the fault.
The coal lying unbroken over the fault means the fault formed before the coal was deposited.

problemText: A rock outcrop shows six distinct features: three flat, undisturbed layers (siltstone at bottom, then sandstone, then shale); a vertical crack filled with hardened igneous rock that cuts through the siltstone and sandstone but stops before reaching the shale; a second fault that cuts through the siltstone, sandstone, shale, and the igneous rock filling the first crack; and a layer of limestone sitting flat and unbroken across the top of the second fault. Arrange all six features in order from oldest to youngest, and explain which rule or rules you used to place the second fault.
choices: Siltstone, sandstone, igneous crack, shale, limestone, second fault. The second fault is youngest because it cuts through everything else, making it the most recent disturbance.

Siltstone, sandstone, shale, igneous crack, second fault, limestone. The second fault must come after the shale because superposition tells us the shale is younger than the layers below it, and the fault cuts through the shale, so the fault must be even younger than the shale.

Igneous crack, siltstone, sandstone, shale, second fault, limestone. The igneous crack is oldest because it was injected into the rock before any layering occurred, which means it predates all other features in the sequence.

Siltstone, sandstone, igneous crack, shale, second fault, limestone. The second fault is placed after the igneous crack because the fault cuts through it, which means the fault is younger. The limestone comes last because it lies unbroken over the fault.
hints: Apply superposition to the three undisturbed layers first; then use Rule 3 to place each cutting feature based on what it cuts and what lies over it.
Remember that a cutting feature is not automatically the youngest; it is younger than what it cuts but older than what lies unbroken across it.

problemText: A sample of bone is tested using carbon-14 dating. What does the half-life of carbon-14 tell us about the bone sample?
choices: The point in time when exactly half of the bone's original mass has turned into carbon.
The speed at which heat or moisture causes carbon-14 atoms to break apart more quickly than they normally would.
The total number of years the bone will remain in the ground before it completely falls apart.
The fixed amount of time it takes for half of the original carbon-14 atoms in the bone to decay into a different atom.
hints: Half-life is a property of the radioactive element itself, not of the sample's surroundings or how long it stays buried.
Think about what 'half-life' means word by word: 'half' of what, and 'life' as in the span of time.

problemText: A geologist finds an igneous rock and sends a mineral sample from it to a lab for dating. The lab measures the uranium and lead in the mineral and reports an age of 280 million years. Is this a reasonable result for uranium-lead dating, and why or why not?
choices: Yes, because 280 million years falls inside the range where uranium-lead dating produces reliable results.
No, because uranium-lead dating is only used for ages under 50,000 years and cannot measure anything as old as 280 million years.
Yes, because any igneous rock that contains uranium can be dated accurately no matter how old it is.
No, because uranium-lead dating only works on organic material like wood or bone, not on minerals inside rock.
hints: Recall which method is built for very old samples and which is limited to the last 50,000 years.
Uranium-lead dating uses a very long half-life, so it can measure back hundreds of millions to billions of years.

problemText: A sample of burned wood from an ancient campfire is tested and found to have exactly one-eighth of its original carbon-14 remaining. Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years. How many half-lives have passed?
choices: 1 half-life, because one-eighth is less than one-half.
3 half-lives, because one-half times one-half times one-half equals one-eighth.
2 half-lives, because one-eighth is the same as one-quarter of one-quarter.
8 half-lives, because the sample started with a full amount and now has one-eighth remaining.
hints: After each half-life, the amount of parent atoms is multiplied by one-half. Trace through what happens after each step.
One-half of one-half is one-quarter. One-half of one-quarter is one-eighth. How many times did you multiply by one-half?

problemText: A piece of shell is tested using carbon-14 and found to have 3 half-lives' worth of decay. The half-life of carbon-14 is about 5,730 years. Calculate the age of the shell in years, then determine whether this age falls within carbon-14's reliable range and explain why or why not.
choices: The shell is about 1,910 years old and falls within the reliable range because any age under 100,000 years can be dated with carbon-14.

The shell is about 17,190 years old but falls outside the reliable range because carbon-14 becomes too unreliable after more than 10,000 years have passed and too little isotope remains to measure accurately.
The shell is about 17,190 years old and falls within the reliable range because 17,190 years is much less than the roughly 50,000-year limit of carbon-14 dating.

The shell is about 5,730 years old and falls outside the reliable range because after just one half-life passes, the amount of carbon-14 remaining is already too small to produce a dependable age measurement.
hints: Multiply the number of half-lives by the length of one half-life to get the age, then compare the result to carbon-14's known range of about 50,000 years.
Three half-lives means multiply 3 by 5,730. The rule for carbon-14 is that it stays reliable up to about 50,000 years before too little remains to measure.

problemText: A paleontologist discovers a rock layer dated by uranium-lead analysis to be about 75 million years old. Using the Phanerozoic era boundaries (Paleozoic: about 541 to 252 million years ago; Mesozoic: about 252 to 66 million years ago; Cenozoic: about 66 million years ago to today), explain which era this rock layer belongs to and why uranium-lead dating, not carbon-14, was the correct choice for this rock.
choices: The rock belongs to the Paleozoic Era because that era lasted the longest. Uranium-lead was correct because it works for any material, while carbon-14 only works for organic material like bone and wood.

The rock belongs to the Cenozoic Era because that is the most recent era. Uranium-lead was correct because it can measure ages of millions of years, while carbon-14 is only reliable up to about 50,000 years.

The rock belongs to the Mesozoic Era because it has decayed more than rocks from the Cenozoic but less than rocks from the Paleozoic Era. Uranium-lead was correct because carbon-14 works only for organic material, not for the mineral compounds in rocks.

The rock belongs to the Mesozoic Era. Uranium-lead was correct because it is the only method that can accurately measure ages of millions of years, while carbon-14 is only reliable up to about 50,000 years.
hints: Line up your numbers carefully: 75 million is between 252 million and 66 million, so compare those boundaries to place the era.
Think about why we use different methods for different materials and age ranges, not just which one is always right for rock.

problemText: A scientist measures a fossil bone and finds it contains 1 part per 16 of its original carbon-14. Before she calculates the age, she wants to check whether carbon-14 is even the right method for this fossil. Explain why or why not carbon-14 is appropriate, and calculate the number of years that have passed, showing your reasoning about the half-lives. Carbon-14's half-life is about 5,730 years.
choices: Carbon-14 is appropriate because bone is once-living material. Four half-lives have passed (1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/16), so the age is about 22,920 years, which is well within carbon-14's reliable range of about 50,000 years.

Carbon-14 is not appropriate because bone contains minerals that require uranium-lead dating instead. Even if we calculated an age by dividing half-lives, the result would be unreliable because carbon-14 does not work for mineral samples.

Carbon-14 is appropriate because bone is once-living material, but the fossil is too old for accurate dating. Five half-lives have passed (1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/32), so the age is about 28,650 years, which far exceeds carbon-14's reliable limit of roughly 50,000 years.

Carbon-14 is appropriate because bone is derived from living organisms, but too many half-lives have passed. Three half-lives have passed (1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8), so the age is about 17,190 years, but this exceeds the point where carbon-14 atoms are too scarce to measure reliably.
hints: Bone comes from a once-living animal, so it matches the material carbon-14 is designed for. Write out the fractions as products to count the half-lives: start with 1 and keep multiplying by 1/2 until you reach 1/16.
Once you know the number of half-lives, multiply by 5,730 years per half-life to get the age, then ask whether that result makes sense for carbon-14's known limit.

problemText: Which three characteristics make a fossil useful as an index fossil for dating rock layers?
choices: It lived during a narrow window of time, spread across a wide geographic area, and has a distinctive shape that is easy to tell apart from other species.
It is found in the oldest rocks on Earth, appears in layers that are easy to dig through, and is common enough that scientists can find many specimens.
It lived in deep ocean water, was very large compared to modern animals, and left behind hard shells or bones that preserve well.
It is found in only one location, lived for a very long time, and looks similar to many other fossil species from different time periods.
hints: Think about what makes a fossil useful as a time marker rather than what makes it easy to find or preserve.
A good index fossil needs to pin down a narrow time window, be found in many places, and be unmistakable.

problemText: A rock layer contains fossils of an extinct trilobite species. Previous absolute dating shows this trilobite lived only between 490 million and 485 million years ago. Based on this information alone, what can you conclude about when the rock layer formed?
choices: The layer formed exactly 487.5 million years ago, the midpoint of the trilobite's time range.
The layer formed sometime within the 5-million-year window from 490 to 485 million years ago, but not necessarily at one exact year.
The layer must be older than 490 million years, because trilobites went extinct before the layer was deposited.
The layer formed during a time when trilobites were becoming less common, based on how the fossils are distributed in the rock.
hints: An index fossil gives you a window of time, not one precise moment.
Remember: a 5-million-year window is what the fossil tells you; getting one exact year would require radiometric dating of the rock itself.

problemText: A geologist is trying to pick the best index fossil from four options to use for dating layers in a region. Option A lived only from 200 to 195 million years ago but was found in only one small valley. Option B lived from 300 to 100 million years ago and was spread across many continents. Option C lived from 75 to 70 million years ago, spread across an entire continent, and looks almost identical to another species from 65 to 60 million years ago. Option D lived from 88 to 82 million years ago, spread across multiple continents, and has a very distinctive shape. Which option would make the poorest choice?
choices: Option A, because its time range is too narrow to be useful.
Option C, because it is easy to confuse with a similar-looking species from a different time.
Option B, because its time range is too wide to narrow down the age of a layer much.
Option D, because it lived in an ocean environment instead of on land.
hints: A fossil that lived during a huge span of geologic time does not narrow down the age window much.
Think about which fossil would tell you the least about when a layer formed.

problemText: On two different continents separated by thousands of kilometers, geologists find the same species of extinct spiral-shelled sea creature in rock layers that have no visible physical connection. Previous absolute dating shows this species lived only between 105 million and 100 million years ago. One continent's layer sits near the bottom of a deep rock stack, while the other continent's layer sits near the top of its own separate stack. What two different conclusions can the geologist draw from this discovery, and what is one thing the fossil does not tell you?
choices: The bottom layer was deposited 105 million years ago and the top layer was deposited 100 million years ago based on their positions in their respective stacks, and the shared fossil proves the two continents had similar climates.
The layer near the bottom must be older than the layer near the top because it is lower in its rock stack, and the shared fossil proves that both organisms lived at the bottom of the ocean.

The two layers sit right next to each other in the global rock record even though they are on different continents, and the fossil shows that the species itself did not change its appearance between the two locations.

Both layers must have formed within the same 5-million-year window, showing that index fossils can match separated layers by age; however, the fossil does not say whether the two locations had the same environment at the time.
hints: Correlation means matching layers from different locations using a shared fossil as a time marker—what does that ability let you conclude?
Remember what a fossil's age window does and does not tell you about the places and organisms involved.

problemText: A geologist studying two rock layers in a single unbroken cliff stack uses the order of the layers (law of superposition) to determine that the lower layer is older. Now suppose the same two layers, with identical fossil contents, are found on opposite sides of a wide mountain range with no visible connection between them. Would using an index fossil from those layers to correlate them give the same conclusion about their age order, a different conclusion, or no useful conclusion at all? Explain your reasoning.
choices: It would give the same conclusion about their relative age order, but only if the fossil's known time range is narrow enough that it actually narrows down the window—otherwise, a fossil shared by both layers just confirms both fall within the same (perhaps very wide) time window without saying which is older.

It would give a different conclusion because the fossil method works only for layers deposited on the same landmass, and the mountain range creates a physical barrier that prevents index fossil correlation from being reliable across geographic separation.

It would give no useful conclusion because an index fossil can only tell you that both separated layers lived during overlapping or identical time periods, but cannot determine which of the two layers is actually older without positional information.

It would give a different conclusion because the law of superposition applies only to layers at one location, and fossil evidence alone cannot reveal the relative age order of layers that are geographically disconnected from each other.
hints: What does an index fossil tell you about two separated layers, and what does position tell you that a fossil alone cannot?
An index fossil can confirm that both layers fall in the same time window, but remember what it does and does not do compared to the stacking order of layers in one place.

problemText: A paleontologist finds three rock layers at a single location. The bottom layer contains an index fossil known to have lived from 300 to 295 million years ago. The middle layer contains an index fossil known to have lived from 290 to 285 million years ago. The top layer contains an index fossil known to have lived from 288 to 283 million years ago. The top two layers' time ranges overlap (288 to 285 million years ago). If all three layers were deposited in an unbroken stack with no mixing or disturbance, which statement best describes what happened and what you can conclude?
choices: The layers were deposited out of order, so you cannot trust the fossil evidence because the law of superposition must have been violated.

The bottom layer formed between 300 and 295 million years ago; the middle layer formed between 290 and 285 million years ago; the top layer formed during the overlap window from 288 to 285 million years ago, consistent with the undisturbed stacking order.
The top two layers must have formed at the same time because their time ranges overlap, so they cannot be separated by age using fossils alone.
The overlapping ranges of the top two layers prove that one of the index fossils was misidentified, because properly dated layers in an unbroken stack should never have overlapping time windows.
hints: Check whether each fossil's known time range is consistent with the order you see in the rock stack from bottom to top.
An index fossil gives a window of possible ages for a layer—does that window have to be completely separate from the windows of layers above and below it?

problemText: A mass-extinction boundary is a sudden, worldwide change in the fossil record where certain fossil types stop appearing and different ones take their place. What makes this change useful as a time marker for matching rock layers from different parts of the world?
choices: The fossil types that disappear are always the oldest fossils in the rock record, so any boundary that removes them must mark the same moment everywhere.

The same abrupt change shows up at the same relative position in rock layers thousands of kilometers apart, so geologists can match layers formed at the same time without needing a direct age in years.
The new fossil types that appear after the boundary are always larger and more diverse than the ones that came before, making them easy to spot.
Geologists can measure the exact age in years of any boundary by counting the layers between it and the surface of the rock.
hints: Think about why the same change in different places thousands of kilometers apart would be useful for matching time.
Does the boundary have to be dated in years for it to be a useful time marker?

problemText: A geologist finds a rock layer where a large share of the shell fossils that were common in lower layers suddenly stop appearing, and different shell types become common in layers above it. The geologist observes this same sudden change at a second location thousands of kilometers away, at the same relative position in the rock sequence. Based only on the pattern described, what has the geologist found?
choices: Proof that the shell fossils moved from one location to the other over time.
Two different boundaries that happen to look similar because the two locations had the same climate in the past.
A mass-extinction boundary that marks the same moment in time at both locations.
Evidence that the rock layers at the second location are younger than those at the first location.
hints: What does it mean when the same sudden change in fossils appears at the same relative position in two distant places?
Does finding the same pattern in two places tell you about the age in years, or about whether they happened at the same time?

problemText: The five major mass-extinction boundaries, listed from oldest to youngest, are end-Ordovician (about 440 million years ago), end-Devonian (about 360 million years ago), end-Permian (about 250 million years ago), end-Triassic (about 200 million years ago), and end-Cretaceous (about 66 million years ago). In an undisturbed rock sequence, which of these boundaries would you expect to find lowest (deepest) in the stack of layers?
choices: End-Devonian, because it is roughly in the middle of the time range and middle-aged layers settle at the bottom.
End-Permian, because it is the most severe and severe boundaries sink deeper into the rock over time.
End-Cretaceous, because it is the youngest and therefore the most recently buried layer in the sequence.
End-Ordovician, because it is the oldest of the five and superposition places older layers below younger ones.
hints: What rule from earlier lets you predict the order of rock layers in an undisturbed stack?
Does severity (how many fossils disappeared) set the position of a boundary, or does age (how long ago it happened) set it?

problemText: A single, undisturbed rock sequence shows two mass-extinction boundaries, both below the layer that marks the end of the Paleozoic Era. A student claims that the lower of the two boundaries must be end-Permian because end-Permian is the most severe of all five boundaries, so it must be the first one to appear at the bottom. Identify the error in the student's reasoning and state which two boundaries actually sit below the end of the Paleozoic Era.
choices: The error is confusing severity with age. End-Ordovician and end-Devonian sit below the end of the Paleozoic Era; both are less severe than end-Permian but older than it.
The error is confusing location with boundary type. End-Permian and end-Triassic sit below the end of the Paleozoic Era; they are period boundaries, not era boundaries.
The error is assuming that older layers always contain the largest fossils. End-Cretaceous and end-Triassic sit below the end of the Paleozoic Era because they preserve smaller fossil types.
The error is not recognizing that end-Permian is an era boundary. End-Ordovician and end-Triassic sit below the end of the Paleozoic Era because era boundaries always come in pairs.
hints: Severity and age are two separate facts. Does knowing a boundary is the most severe tell you whether it is old or young?
Which two of the five boundaries are actually older than end-Permian and sit inside the Paleozoic Era?

problemText: The end-Cretaceous boundary, about 66 million years ago, separates the Mesozoic Era from the Cenozoic Era. The end-Permian boundary, about 250 million years ago, separates the Paleozoic Era from the Mesozoic Era. Using the order of the five boundaries, which of the following statements about the Mesozoic Era must be true?
choices: The Mesozoic Era contains all five boundaries within it because the boundaries mark divisions at multiple levels of geologic time.
The Mesozoic Era began at the end-Permian boundary and ended at the end-Cretaceous boundary, so it includes the end-Triassic boundary but not the end-Devonian boundary.
The Mesozoic Era spans from the end-Ordovician boundary to the end-Cretaceous boundary because those are the first and last extinction events.
The Mesozoic Era is longer than the Paleozoic Era because it includes more boundaries and therefore more divisions into periods.
hints: An era boundary marks the start and end of an era. What are the era boundaries for the Mesozoic?
Of the five boundaries, which ones fall between the end-Permian and end-Cretaceous boundaries?

problemText: Two geologists study rock outcrops in different countries. Outcrop A contains three mass-extinction boundaries; the oldest sits about 200 meters below the layer marking the end of the Paleozoic Era, the middle one sits about 100 meters below it, and the youngest sits about 10 meters below it. Outcrop B contains only two of the five major boundaries, both below the end-Paleozoic-Era layer. Outcrop B's lower boundary is older than 400 million years ago, and its upper boundary is younger than 350 million years ago. Which boundary is missing from Outcrop B, and why can you determine this without knowing the exact meter-depths in Outcrop B?
choices: End-Triassic is missing from Outcrop B. Outcrop B's age range of 400 to 350 million years ago falls entirely within the Mesozoic Era, so no Paleozoic boundaries can exist there; end-Triassic is the only Mesozoic boundary that could be missing.

End-Ordovician is missing from Outcrop B. The Paleozoic Era contains three boundaries below its end, so the three deepest boundaries overall must be end-Ordovician, end-Devonian, and end-Permian; if Outcrop B only has two, the missing one must be end-Ordovician because it is the least severe.

End-Devonian is missing from Outcrop B. End-Ordovician (about 440 mya) and end-Devonian (about 360 mya) are the two boundaries in the Paleozoic Era below the end-Paleozoic-Era layer; end-Devonian must be the younger boundary in Outcrop B's range, but the age range given (older than 400 mya, younger than 350 mya) does not include 360 mya.

End-Permian is missing from Outcrop B. The end-Paleozoic-Era layer is another name for the end-Permian boundary, so Outcrop B cannot contain any boundary younger than end-Permian; since Outcrop B has two boundaries below that layer, end-Permian itself is the missing one.
hints: Which two of the five boundaries are older than the end of the Paleozoic Era and sit below it?
Does the age range 400 to 350 million years ago include both 440 mya and 360 mya, or is one of them outside the range?
